## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/12.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Accountability and Outcomes
• The central focus of educational accountability systems since NCLB has been academic outcomes,
 largely derived from large scale, state administered summative assessments.
• Student academic proficiency has been the main determinant of education quality.
 • NCLB mandated universal proficiency (100% proficient) by 2014
 • ESSA mandates more modest proficiency targets.
• I am highly critical of the way that educational accountability has been conceived over the last two
 decades, but not for the reasons you might think:
 • I am a strong proponent of annual, large scale, summative assessments.
 • I am a strong proponent of reporting achievement outcomes like student academic proficiency (I.e.,
 percent proficient)
• Outcomes from large scale, standardized summative assessments like academic proficiency are
 important, but there’s a rub.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/13.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">The Problem
• Not all outcomes derived from state summative assessments are created equal.
 • Distal outcomes: Achievement/attainment such as academic proficiency
 • Proximal outcomes: Growth/learning such as student growth percentiles (SGP)
• Growth &amp; Achievement (Learning &amp; Attainment) are often treated as conceptually separate but they are
 intricately related: Growth/Learning leads to Achievement/Attainment
• A desire for high achieving students is necessarily a desire for students who grow/learn a lot and vice-
 versa.
• I often say Growth/Learning and Achievement/Attainment are opposite sides of the same coin.
• Current accountability systems ignore this relationship between growth and achievement and often
 present growth and achievement as a value-laden choice (“Which do you prefer, growth or
 achievement?”)
• Treating growth and achievement separately leads to system incoherence: Desired outcomes (proficiency)
 are divorced from the efforts of teachers, schools, … to support and maximize the learning of students.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/15.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Remember:

Know what you want to accomplish
and focus on the process rather
than the outcome.
 Nick Saban

 • Yes, we want all students to be proficient.
 • That’s analogous to declaring that we want to win all
 of our games.
 • Accomplishing such goals requires a focus on process
 (highly effective processes).
 • The process by which students become proficient is
 learning.
 • Coherent accountability focuses on student learning
 without losing sight of the end goal of student
 proficiency.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/16.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Student Growth
• Student growth connects process with outcomes.
• Student growth is to learning as student attainment is to achievement.
• It is important to note that no single assessment measures student learning/growth.
• Assessments (plural), including MSSA, measure achievement/attainment: What a student knows
 and can do at a given point in time.
• Learning is a process that happens over time.
• We use multiple assessments of achievement to infer whether or not learning has occurred.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/18.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Student Growth/Learning:

If you care about student achievement,
 then you care about student growth.

• Where you are is a function of
 where you started and how quickly
 you’ve travelled since.
• Student growth and student
 attainment/achievement are
 related in this way.
• Distance=Rate x Time
• Those who start behind tend to stay
 behind and those that start ahead
 tend to stay ahead.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/19.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Student Growth - Calculations
• There is a common misconception that because student growth can be difficult to calculate it is difficult to
 understand.

• Calculations may be complicated but knowing how to calculate student growth is not synonymous with
 understanding student growth:
 – The number π (pi=3.14159…) is difficult to calculate but is simple to understand conceptually.
 – Height and weight percentiles associated with children are difficult to calculate but are simple to
 understand conceptually.
 – Credit scores are difficult to calculate but we all know what they mean practically.

• Computational details are important but often obscure a simple conceptual basis.
• Not knowing how something is calculated does not imply that one cannot understand the quantities.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/21.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Student Growth
• Growth as an amount of change:
 – What could be more simple?
 – Like height or weight just calculate the amount of change.
 – Requires a vertical scale (which New Mexico DOESN’T have).
 – Growth = Score Time 2 - Score Time 1
• Not as simple as it seems:
 – Comparisons between students often leads to wrong conclusions.
 – Interpreting change requires context.
 – Even if New Mexico MSSA had a vertical scale, you’ll see that it doesn’t give you want you
 think.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/24.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Student Growth
• The same holds true for the vertically scaled tests (e.g., SBAC).

 Average Scale Score Change 2022 to 2023

 Top 10% ELA Grade 4 2023: -7.5
 Bottom 10% ELA Grade 4 2023: +24.5
 Top 10% Mathematic Grade 4 2023: -12.6
 Bottom 10% Mathematics Grade 4 2023: +18.4

• Large increases for the lowest 10% of achievers, small (negative) increases for high achievers.
• Just as an inch isn’t necessarily an inch; a scale score point isn’t necessarily a scale score point.
• Moral of the story: There’s more to student growth than subtraction (and in New Mexico you
 aren’t supposed to subtract student scores with the MSSA)</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/25.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Student Growth
• This is analogous to height/weight measures for infants.
• Growth amounts are tricky to interpret and require context.
• Peer based comparisons used by growth analyses are a way to acquire
 that context.

 An infant male toddler is measured at 2 and 3 years of age
 and is shown to have grown 4 inches. The magnitude of increase—4
 inches—is a well understood quantity that any parent can grasp and
 calculate at home using a simple yardstick. However, parents
 leaving their pediatrician’s office knowing only how much their child
 has grown would likely be wanting for more information: Parents are
 not interested in an absolute magnitude of growth, but instead in a
 norm-referenced quantity locating that 4 inch increase alongside the
 height increases of similar children.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/26.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Student Growth
• Peer-based analyses are also called norm-referenced analyses.
• Like with infant height/weight charts, peers are children/student with
 similar characteristics.
• For growth analyses using large scale assessments, peers are students with
 (at least) the same scale score history on the same tests.
• Peer based norms are invaluable in providing context for stakeholders to
 understand student growth.
• Peer based norms are possible even across test content areas or test
 transitions.
• This is the mathematical basis of Student Growth Percentiles, as the
 following slides illustrate.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/34.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Student Growth
• Peer-based growth calculations are only as good as the assessments on which they are
 based.
• With quality assessments, peer based analyses can allow for all students to
 demonstrate growth.
• However, ceiling or floor effects on a test can impede the analysis of growth for students
 at the extremes.
• The goal is to be able to allow various stakeholders groups to investigates student
 growth/learning and answer questions relevant to them.
• What are some of these questions (Yen, 2007).</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/35.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Relevant Questions for Parents
• Did my child make a year’s worth of learning in a year?
• Is my child growing appropriately toward meeting state standards?
• Is my child growing as much in Math as Reading?
• Did my child grow as much this year as last year?</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/43.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Changing conversations about education
 • Accountability together with disconnected point in me assessments have
 led to a focus on outcomes (achievement) at the expense of learning/
 growth.
 • This focus has led to incoherence in the way we understand the
 performance of our educa on systems and the way in which we hold them
 accountable.
 • How much students grow/learn is directly connected to later levels of
 achievement in the same way velocity is related to distance traveled.
 • The purpose of New Mexico’s Growth Model/SGPs is to make these
 connec ons apparent and change stakeholder conversa ons about
 educa on and student performance.
```
